name: I STILTON HAVEN'T FOUND WHAT THYME LOOKING FOR BURGER

recipe.history:
Stilton is the king of British cheeses, a blue-veined wheel of raw or pasteurized cow's milk that can legally be produced in only three English counties — Derbyshire, Leicestershire, and Nottinghamshire — under a Protected Designation of Origin that makes it one of only a handful of British foods to carry that status. Its recorded history begins in the early eighteenth century, when it was sold at the Bell Inn in the town of Stilton in Cambridgeshire — a coaching town on the Great North Road — giving it the name it bears today, despite the fact that it was never actually made there. The making of Stilton requires the piercing of the young cheese with stainless steel needles to introduce oxygen, encouraging the growth of Penicillium roqueforti — the blue-green mold that develops through the paste in distinctive veins — and the cheese is then aged for nine to twelve weeks, during which time it develops its characteristic bold, pungent, complex flavor: simultaneously sharp and rich, salty and sweet, with a slightly crumbly paste that softens to cream around the edges of the rind. A great Stilton, eaten at room temperature with a good cracker or a piece of walnut bread, is one of the most complete sensory experiences available in a food that costs less than twenty dollars.

Blue cheese on burgers entered the American consciousness primarily through the steakhouse tradition, where Roquefort butter — the French blue cheese equivalent of the herb butter — was applied to filets and strips as a finishing element, the rich saltiness of the cheese amplifying the umami of the beef. Stilton specifically began appearing on premium burger menus in the 2000s, as British and Irish pub culture filtered into American cities and the Ploughman's lunch sensibility — the idea of pairing strong cheese with bread and pickles — translated naturally to the burger format. Thyme's pairing with Stilton is a classical one in British cooking, where the herb grows wild in hedgerows and on chalk downland and has been used to season cheese, bread, and roasted meats for centuries. The two things have a natural affinity: thyme's warm, slightly medicinal floral quality cuts through the richness and sharpens the complexity of the blue.

I first paired Stilton and thyme on a burger during a period when I was reading a lot about British farmhouse cheese and had ordered a wedge of Montgomery's Cheddar and a piece of Colston Bassett Stilton by mail, which felt extravagant at the time and now seems entirely sensible. The Stilton was spectacular — deeply veined, almost orange at the rind, creamy and bold — and I ate most of it standing at the counter before I saved enough to crumble over a patty. I had thyme growing in a pot on the windowsill, and I made a quick thyme-infused butter to rest the patty on while it cooked, and when the Stilton melted and the butter perfumed the meat and the whole thing came together between a toasted bun, I thought: yes, this is what Stilton has been waiting for all along. A burger as a vehicle for one of the world's great cheeses.

Stilton does something remarkable to a medium rare patty that it cannot do to a well-done one: it melts unevenly, pooling in some places and remaining crumbly in others, creating pockets of intense blue saltiness against the pink, fatty, yielding interior of the meat. This is not a flaw; it is the entire point. The contrast of textures — melted cheese, crumbled cheese, soft meat — is what makes Stilton on a burger a different experience than any other cheese on any other burger. Cook the patty well-done and you eliminate the soft yielding interior that makes the contrast possible. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the patty has exactly the right texture to receive Stilton in all its unruly complexity. Medium rare is not just a temperature. It is a structural requirement.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
2 tbsp fresh thyme leaves, finely chopped
1 small clove garlic, minced to a paste
For the Stilton crumble and melt:
200g Stilton cheese, at room temperature, crumbled
instructions: 1. Make the thyme compound butter: Combine softened butter, thyme, rosemary, garlic paste, lemon zest, salt, and pepper until thoroughly combined. Roll onto plastic wrap, form into a log, and refrigerate at least 2 hours. Can be made up to 1 week ahead.

2. Make the candied walnuts: Melt butter in a small skillet over medium heat. Add walnuts, brown sugar, cayenne, and salt. Stir constantly for 3–4 minutes until the sugar has melted and caramelized, coating the walnuts. Pour onto a parchment-lined plate, spreading into a single layer. Cool completely — they will harden as they cool. Roughly chop before using.
3. Make the thyme-honey mustard: Stir together both mustards, honey, thyme leaves, white wine vinegar, and black pepper until combined. Refrigerate until ready to use.

4. Prepare the Stilton: Combine crumbled Stilton with heavy cream in a small bowl and work together with a fork until the cheese is still crumbly but slightly more cohesive. Leave at room temperature so it can melt more readily on the hot patty.

5. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
6. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.
7. Divide into 4 equal portions. Shape into smooth balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 45 minutes.
8. Brush buns with egg wash and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

9. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions of about 170g each. Form into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
11. Remove from heat. Immediately top each patty with a generous heap of the Stilton and cream mixture. Cover the pan with a lid for 60 seconds — the residual heat will begin to melt the Stilton.

12. Transfer patties to a resting rack. Slice two rounds of thyme compound butter (about 1/4 inch thick each) and place on top of each patty alongside the melting Stilton. Rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
13. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

14. Assemble: Spread thyme-honey mustard on both cut surfaces of each bun. Place radicchio or frisée on the bottom bun. Set the patty with melted Stilton and thyme butter on the lettuce. Add thin pear slices over the cheese. Scatter candied walnut pieces over the pear. Add a small sprig of fresh thyme. Finish with flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately.
